hints: Focus on the general formula for each homologous series, not just one example, and count how many H you get per C.
Write the simplest general formulas: alcohols are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$, aldehydes are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}$ and acids are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}_2$.
Compare the H to C ratios by dividing through by n, and see which series keeps an extra +2 hydrogens on top of the 2n base.
walkthrough:
**Recall what H to C ratio means**

Think of it as (number of H atoms) divided by (number of C atoms) in the general formula. The more saturated the series, the more H it can hold per C.

Ratio = $$\frac{\text{number of H}}{\text{number of C}}$$

**Write the general formulas**

Let us write each class with n carbons. This makes comparison fair and easy.

Alcohols: $$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+1}\text{OH} = \text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$$

Aldehydes: $$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}$$

Carboxylic acids: $$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}_2$$

Halogenoalkanes (monosubstituted): $$\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+1}\text{X}$$

**Compare the ratios and decide**

Now divide H by C for each:

Alcohols: $$\frac{2n+2}{n} = 2 + \frac{2}{n}$$

Aldehydes: $$\frac{2n}{n} = 2$$

Acids: $$\frac{2n}{n} = 2$$

Halogenoalkanes: $$\frac{2n+1}{n} = 2 + \frac{1}{n}$$

Alcohols have the largest extra term, $2/n$, so they have the highest H to C ratio. The oxygen in $\text{-OH}$ does not replace a hydrogen from the alkane skeleton, while $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-X}$ do.

options.A: Correct. Alcohols follow $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}\text{O}$, the same H count as an alkane. The O inserts into the chain as -OH without removing extra H, giving ratio $2 + 2/n$, which is higher than any other class listed.
options.B: Incorrect. Aldehydes are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}$. The C=O double bond removes two H compared to an alkane, so the ratio is only 2. Students sometimes forget that unsaturation lowers the H count.
options.C: Incorrect. Carboxylic acids are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}\text{O}_2$. Like aldehydes, the C=O plus the -OH on the same carbon gives only 2 H per C on average. The extra O does not add extra H.
options.D: Incorrect. Halogenoalkanes are $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+1}\text{X}$. The halogen X replaces one H from the alkane $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$, so the ratio is $2 + 1/n$. This is high, but still lower than alcohols which keep all $2n+2$ hydrogens.
